questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Splicing Choices Change Message Length
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one gene can give protein variants of different lengths
questions.stem: The clinic's diagnostic brief notes that one gene can produce several protein variants of different lengths. Which process best explains that outcome?

options.text: The pre-messenger RNA is cut and rejoined in different ways, so different exon sets reach the ribosome.
options.misconception: describes the mature message as identical in every case

options.text: The pre-messenger RNA is spliced in more than one way, so the mature messages kept for translation differ in length.
The gene is copied twice within the nucleus and each copy is read in a different reading frame.
options.misconception: invents duplicate gene copies instead of one transcript

options.text: The ribosome starts at a different point on the same message and stops earlier each time.
options.misconception: confuses alternative initiation with alternative splicing

questions.explanation: Alternative splicing keeps different combinations of exons in one pre-messenger RNA, so the mature messages differ in which segments they contain and in length. Re-initiation changes how much is made from one message, not which parts of it are present.
questions.hint: The difference is made before the ribosome arrives.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing Fertiliser Run-Off to a Fish Kill
questions.learningObjective: Calculate nitrogen delivered to a pond from lawn run-off
questions.stem: Rainwater from the lawns around the new wing is routed to a pond that the brief requires to stay clear of fertiliser run-off. The lawn receives 40 grams of fertiliser containing 20 percent nitrogen each week, and the collection catches 30 percent of what falls on the lawn. How many grams of nitrogen reach the pond each week?
questions.explanation: The lawn receives 40 grams of fertiliser carrying 20 percent nitrogen, which is 8 grams of nitrogen, and the collection takes 30 percent of that, giving 2.4 grams reaching the pond each week. Applying the two percentages in turn keeps them separate.
questions.hint: Apply the nitrogen percentage, then the collection fraction.

options.misconception: ignores the large spread between beds

options.text: Nitrogen gains fell as the seasons progressed, so repeated planting exhausts the soil.
options.misconception: reads a seasonal trend into three unrelated beds

questions.explanation: The bed with the largest gain is the one carrying legumes, whose root bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use. That adds nitrogen to the soil rather than removing it, which is why the rotation is proposed.

Water is entering the cell by osmosis because the cell's water potential is lower than the pond's.
options.misconception: confuses the direction of osmosis with a low water potential

options.text: Water is leaving the cell by active transport because the cell is pumping water outwards.
options.misconception: invents an active water pump

options.text: Water is entering the cell by osmosis because the pond's solute is more concentrated than the cell's.
options.misconception: reads the concentration the wrong way round

questions.explanation: In a freshwater cell the cytoplasm holds more solute than the surrounding water, so its water potential is lower and water moves out to the pond. The cell must keep expelling water or it would swell and burst.

questions.learningObjective: Correct a wrong expectation about adding predators to a pond
questions.stem: One pond in the brief was stocked with more predatory fish to improve the fishery, and the plan expects more fish overall. Which correction applies?

options.text: The plan is right, because more predators always means more fish in the pond.
options.misconception: assumes adding predators adds fish

options.text: The plan is right, because predation pressure does not change the numbers of the prey of the prey.
options.misconception: ignores the indirect effects of predation

options.text: Removing predators can release the small fish from predation, so their numbers rise and their prey fall further.
The correction is that predators should be added only after the small fish have been removed entirely.
options.misconception: proposes removing prey instead of reasoning about the cascade

questions.explanation: Predators eat the small fish, which in turn eat the invertebrates. Removing the predators lets the small fish multiply and strip the invertebrates out, so a change at the top of the food web cascades downwards through several levels.
questions.hint: Follow the effect on the levels below the small fish.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Salt Lost in Sweat as a Molarity Step
questions.learningObjective: Explain why sweating removes salt and leads to dehydration
questions.stem: Explain in writing why sweating on a hot site loses salt and why that can leave a worker dehydrated even when water is available.

answer.exemplar: Sweat is produced by the sweat glands as a solution close to blood in salt content, with sodium and chloride as the main solutes. The glands actively reabsorb most of the salt back into the blood as the sweat passes along, but not all of it, so the fluid that finally leaves the body is still salty. Losing that salt draws water from the body to replace it, so salt and water must be replaced together.

questions.explanation: The glands reclaim most but not all of the salt, and the remainder leaves in the sweat. Because that salt sits outside the cells, replacing it with water draws water out of the body, so salt and water must be replaced together.
questions.hint: Some salt is reclaimed by the gland and some is not.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing Heat Through a Leaf's Chemistry
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of how much heat a leaf's chemistry absorbs
questions.stem: Design an experiment that would show how much heat a leaf's chemistry absorbs from sunlight in the brief's courtyard.

answer.exemplar: Measure the temperature of a leaf, of a leaf with its upper surface covered with a transparent film, and of a bare thermometer in the same sunlight for the same time, and repeat with the light switched off. The difference between the lit and dark readings gives the energy taken up by the leaf, and comparing the covered leaf with the untreated one shows how much of that is captured by the light reactions.

questions.explanation: A dark control separates the energy absorbed from the heat of the surroundings, and the covered leaf separates the light-driven chemistry from plain heating. The three readings together partition the energy the leaf takes up.
questions.hint: Include a dark control and a covered leaf.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Cold Slowing Membrane Transport
questions.learningObjective: Explain why cold storage slows membrane transport
questions.stem: Several chilled rooms in the brief hold biological samples at 4 degrees, and the facilities note that transport in those samples is slower than at 20 degrees. What causes this?

options.text: Cold freezes the membrane, so the lipids turn into rigid crystals that block transport.
options.misconception: treats chill temperatures as freezing

options.text: Cold reduces the concentration of solutes inside the cells, so there is less left to transport.
options.misconception: invents a concentration change to explain the slowdown

options.text: Cold makes the cells pump water out, so the inside becomes concentrated and transport stops.
options.misconception: describes a stress response instead of a temperature effect

options.text: Lower temperature reduces the movement of membrane lipids and proteins, so the transport they carry is slower.

questions.explanation: Membrane lipids and proteins move more slowly at low temperature, and both facilitated diffusion and pumping depend on that movement. Refrigeration therefore slows transport rather than stopping it, and at 4 degrees the membranes remain fluid.
questions.hint: Think about how temperature affects molecular movement.

options.misconception: treats nitrate as a dilution effect

options.misconception: denies osmotic water entry

options.text: Each cell expels the water that enters by osmosis, so water balance holds at the level of the whole cell.
The correction is that the cells swell until the pond's concentration matches the cell's.
options.misconception: expects the pond to be diluted to cell level

options.text: The correction is that the pond must be made less dilute to stop water leaving the cells.
options.misconception: proposes changing the pond instead of the cell

questions.explanation: Water keeps entering the cell from the dilute pond and leaving again by an active pump, so each cell holds a constant volume without needing the pond to change. Without that pump the cell would swell and burst.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Reading a Trophic Cascade
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a change in top predators alters plant numbers
questions.stem: Raptors over the estate pond are scarce this year, and the brief asks what that will do to the pond's plant life. Explain in writing how a change in top predators can alter the number of plants.

answer.exemplar: Fewer top predators allow the small fish to increase, and the extra small fish eat more of the grazing invertebrates. With fewer grazers removing plant material, the plant biomass rises, so a change at the top of the food web produces an opposite change at the bottom. Each step of the cascade passes the effect on to the next level down.

questions.explanation: The effect travels down the food web as a chain of changes in numbers, and the final effect on plants can be the reverse of the original change in predators. Recognising that sequence is what makes a cascade predictable.
questions.hint: Follow the chain of who eats whom.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Salt Lost in Sweat as a Molarity Step
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether sweat is hypo, iso or hypertonic
questions.stem: Design an experiment that would show whether the workers' sweat on this site is hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic compared with their blood plasma.

answer.exemplar: Collect sweat from the workers after a period of exercise and measure the concentration of sodium in it, then measure sodium in a blood sample from the same individuals and compare the two values. A sweat sample below, equal to or above the plasma concentration identifies it as hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic, and sampling after rest as well as after exercise shows whether the gland changes its recovery.

questions.explanation: Comparing the solute concentration of sweat with that of plasma from the same people classifies the secretion directly. The comparison must be like with like, since the plasma value itself changes with hydration during the exercise.
questions.hint: Compare sweat with blood from the same individuals.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Ordering a Freshwater Cell's Water Problem
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a freshwater cell avoids swelling and bursting
questions.stem: Explain in writing why a freshwater cell in the brief's pond does not swell and burst, and what would happen without its adaptations.

answer.exemplar: Because the surrounding water is dilute, water enters the cell by osmosis, so the cell must remove it again. Its contractile vacuole collects the excess and expels it, and the cell wall restrains the surface so that expansion cannot rupture the membrane. Without the pump the cell would swell, and without the wall the expanding membrane would burst.

questions.explanation: Two separate features handle the problem: an active pump removes the incoming water and a rigid wall prevents expansion from bursting the membrane. Removing either one alone leaves the cell exposed to osmotic damage.
questions.hint: Name both the pump and the wall.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Reading a Trophic Cascade
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of a predicted trophic cascade in the pond
questions.stem: Plans for the pond include removing the top predators. Design an experiment that would test the predicted cascade before the change is made.

answer.exemplar: Before any fish are removed, record the numbers of predators, small fish, grazing invertebrates and plant biomass in the pond, then remove the predators and repeat the same counts at regular intervals, alongside a comparable pond that is left unchanged. If plant biomass rises and invertebrates fall only in the treated pond, the cascade is supported and the control rules out seasonal effects.

questions.explanation: Recording the whole food web before and after the change captures every step of the cascade rather than only the top and bottom. A second pond left unchanged separates the cascade from ordinary seasonal change in the water.
questions.hint: Record every level, and keep a second pond as a control.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing Fixed Nitrogen Through a Community
questions.learningObjective: Explain how atmospheric nitrogen becomes part of the plants
questions.stem: Explain in writing how nitrogen from the air becomes part of the plants growing in the brief's grounds.

answer.exemplar: Nitrogen gas in the air is chemically very unreactive, so it must be converted before plants can use it. Bacteria in the root nodules of legumes use an enzyme to split the gas into ammonia, which is passed to the plant and built into amino acids, while the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars from photosynthesis. When the legumes decompose, that nitrogen enters the soil for other plants.

questions.explanation: Fixation converts an unusable gas into ammonia that the plant can build into amino acids. The exchange is mutual, since the plant gives the bacteria sugars, and the fixed nitrogen later reaches the wider soil community when the plant dies.
questions.hint: The gas must be converted before it can be used.

answer.exemplar: Grow identical pondweed samples under a range of water pressures by varying the depth at which they sit, then measure cell volume, the rate of water expulsion and the state of the contractile vacuole in each. Cells under greater pressure should expel water faster and hold a smaller volume, and any cell that cannot keep up should begin to swell and burst.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing Fertiliser Run-Off to a Fish Kill
questions.learningObjective: Explain how lawn fertiliser can kill fish in a pond
questions.stem: Explain in writing how fertiliser applied to the lawns can end up killing fish in the brief's pond.

answer.exemplar: Rain falls on grass that has been treated with fertiliser, dissolves the soluble salts and runs across the surface towards the pond. The pond then receives a pulse of nitrate and phosphate, which fertilises algae so strongly that the algae die, and the bacteria decomposing them use up the dissolved oxygen the fish need to breathe, suffocating the fish in the water that was enriched.

questions.explanation: The chain runs from soluble salts, to algal overgrowth, to oxygen depletion as the algae rot. The fish die of low oxygen rather than of the fertiliser itself, which is why the damage appears after the bloom rather than at once.
questions.hint: Follow the nutrients into the water and then the oxygen.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Splicing Choices Change Message Length
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one gene yields variants of different lengths
questions.stem: Explain in writing how one gene can give rise to protein variants of different lengths in the clinic's samples.

answer.exemplar: The gene's pre-messenger RNA is cut and rejoined at different splice sites in different cells, so the mature messages kept for translation contain different combinations of exons. Because the exons differ in length as well as in number, each mature message is a different length and specifies a different protein variant, which is why one gene can yield several assay bands.

questions.explanation: The variation is made at splicing, after the gene has been copied but before translation. Different exon choices give messages of different lengths and so different protein products from one unchanged sequence.
questions.hint: The choice is made between copying and translation.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Cold Slowing Membrane Transport
questions.learningObjective: Explain why chilling slows membrane transport processes
questions.stem: Explain in writing why the chillers in the brief slow down the transport processes in stored samples.

answer.exemplar: Transport across a membrane depends on the movement of lipids and proteins, and both move more slowly when the temperature falls, because they have less kinetic energy. A lowered temperature therefore slows facilitated diffusion, slows the opening and closing of channels, and slows the conformational cycling that carriers use. Nothing has to freeze for the rates to drop noticeably, which is why chilled storage extends the useful life of a sample.

questions.explanation: The rate of membrane processes follows molecular movement, and movement slows as temperature falls. Because no membrane has to freeze, the effect is a graded slowdown rather than a switch that stops transport.
questions.hint: The effect is on how fast molecules move.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Splicing Choices Change Message Length
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes some splice variants shorter than others
questions.stem: Variant messenger RNAs from one clinic sample differ in length, and the brief asks what makes some variants shorter than others.

options.text: The shorter variants were cut down afterwards by enzymes that degrade the messenger RNA.
options.misconception: describes degradation rather than selective splicing

options.text: Alternative splicing omits certain exons from the mature message, so the variant keeping fewer of them is shorter.
The shorter variants come from a different gene that was copied from the first one.
options.misconception: invents a duplicate gene as the source

options.text: The shorter variants simply failed to finish being copied, so they are incomplete copies.
options.misconception: treats transcription errors as the normal route

questions.explanation: Splicing removes introns and can also skip particular exons, so choosing fewer exons yields a shorter mature message. Nothing is degraded afterwards and no new gene is involved, since all variants come from the same copied sequence.
questions.hint: Compare which exons each variant keeps.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing Fertiliser Run-Off to a Fish Kill
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the nitrogen mass carried by drainage outflow
questions.stem: Drainage from the new wing's car park is treated before it reaches the pond, and the brief asks how much nitrogen the outflow carries in a week. The drainage volume is 500000 litres and the treated water contains 0.2 milligrams of nitrate nitrogen per litre. How many grams of nitrogen does that outflow carry each week?
questions.explanation: The outflow carries 500000 litres times 0.2 milligrams per litre, which is 100000 milligrams, and that is 100 grams of nitrogen each week. Multiplying concentration by volume gives the delivered mass, which is the figure the brief needs.
questions.hint: Multiply the concentration by the volume and convert units.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing Fixed Nitrogen Through a Community
questions.learningObjective: Interpret soil nitrogen under different crop rotations
questions.stem: Rotation of the grounds' beds is planned so that legumes follow the leafy crops. The brief records soil nitrogen after three years at 40, 68 and 22 kilograms per hectare for legume-first, legume-last and no-legume rotations. Which reading fits?

options.text: The legume-last rotation leaves the most nitrogen, so timing does not matter.
options.misconception: ignores the ordering of the rotation

options.text: All three rotations leave similar nitrogen, so legumes do not change the soil.
options.misconception: ignores a clear difference between rotations

options.text: The no-legume rotation leaves the most nitrogen, so legumes take nitrogen out of the soil.
options.misconception: reverses the role of the legumes

options.text: The legume-first rotation leaves the most soil nitrogen, so the benefit depends on when the legume is grown.

questions.explanation: The legume-first bed carries the most nitrogen, because the crop that follows a fixing plant draws on nitrogen the legume added while it was growing. The benefit therefore depends on where the legume sits in the sequence, not simply on its presence.
questions.hint: Which crop follows the legume in each rotation?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Ordering a Freshwater Cell's Water Problem
questions.learningObjective: Read a pondweed cell diagram of channels and vacuole
questions.stem: Aquaporin channels are drawn in the membrane of a pondweed cell in the brief, with an arrow of water entering and a contractile vacuole drawn at one corner of the cell.

options.text: Channels admit the incoming water quickly and the vacuole expels it, so the cell holds its shape.
The channels expel water directly to the outside, so the vacuole is unnecessary.
options.misconception: assigns the pumping role to the channels

options.text: The channels let solutes in, which would make the cell's water potential more negative still.
options.misconception: gives the channels a solute-transport role

options.text: The vacuole stores water for later use, and the channels are only needed when the cell is drying.
options.misconception: makes the vacuole a storage organ rather than a pump

questions.explanation: The diagram shows two complementary parts: channels that let water in quickly along the gradient and a vacuole that actively expels the surplus. Together they keep the cell's volume steady in dilute water without bursting it.
questions.hint: What do the channels do that the vacuole cannot?
